rounds.proof_sketch: A_tile[i][j] maps to offset i*32+j for both [32][32] and [33][32] arrays. All accesses use threadIdx.y∈[0,31] and k∈[0,31] (from loop 'for(int k=0;k<32;k++)'). Block dim is 32x32, so threadIdx.y is always <32. The stride (32) is determined by the second dimension, which is unchanged. Therefore identical memory locations are accessed in both versions.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation changes A_tile from [32][32] to [33][32], adding an extra row at index 32 that is never accessed. In C/CUDA, 2D array element arr[i][j] is at memory offset i*N+j where N is the second dimension. Since N=32 in both cases, the stride is identical. All writes use A_tile[threadIdx.y][threadIdx.x] where threadIdx.y∈[0,31] (block dimension is 32). All reads use A_tile[threadIdx.y][k] where threadIdx.y∈[0,31] and k∈[0,31] (loop bound is 32). The extra row never participates in any computation. This makes the mutant functionally identical to the original regardless of input values.
rounds.kill_strategy: Unkillable. The mutation only affects memory allocation size, not the memory layout or access pattern of any computed element. The stride (determined by second dimension = 32) is unchanged, so all accessed indices map to identical offsets. No value-level input can distinguish the behavior because the mutation doesn't alter any computation path.
rounds.recommendations: For mutation testing of shared memory array dimensions, mutations to the first dimension of multi-dimensional arrays are often semantically equivalent because they don't affect the stride used in address calculation. More effective mutations would target the second dimension (which affects stride) or the actual indexing expressions. Consider filtering out mutations to first-dimension array sizes when the array access pattern is bounded by other constants.
